# Economic Focus **Catching the global cold** The developed economies of Asia have lost significant momentum over the past few months. Japan, South Korea, Singapore and Taiwan have all seen their exports weaken as demand from key trade partners has softened. With these economies leveraged towards exports, weaker trade is taking its toll on economic growth – especially manufacturing. In short, recession in Europe, slow growth in the US and slowdown in China are giving Asia’s developed economies a cold. Lead indicators offer up few reasons to be optimistic that recovery is imminent; trade, and with it economic growth, will continue to struggle in the coming months. ## **Japanese trade (Billions of yen) South Korean trade (millions of US$)** 8000

**Industrial downturn** Poor manufacturing data has been a feature of Asia’s more developed economies over the past six months. In Japan, industrial production has fallen by 6% since the end of the first quarter, resulting in year-on-year activity down by close to 5%. South Korea has also seen industrial output fall by 4% since the first quarter, while Q3 GDP expanded at its slowest pace since 2009. While industrial output in Taiwan increased slightly over the past quarter, output for the first nine months of 2012 was down by 1.5% from a year earlier. **Exports slump** The lack of growth in exports is the main reason for industrial weakness. South Korean exports have been trending downwards since mid-2011, and through the first three quarters of 2012 have contracted by 1.5% from a year earlier. Almost all of Korea’s main exports, such as cars, ships, machinery and semi-conductors, are down from the level of a year earlier. We have seen a similar trend in Taiwan, with year-to-date exports contracting by 2% year on year. But it is Japan that has arguably suffered the most with Q3 exports down 8.1% year on year. Growth in imports has led to Economic Focus a worsening trade deficit. Japan’s weakness in exports is not just about poor demand in the rest of the world; the continued strength of the yen has reduced Japan’s export competitiveness, often resulting in a loss of export market share. ## **Japanese and Korean exports by destination in 2011** 21%

**Europe to blame?** At first glance, the trade statistics sugg

est that weak demand in China is the primary cause of weak export growth. China is the largest export destination for these Asian economies, and Japanese, Korean and Taiwanese exports to China have fallen so far in 2012 by 10%, 2% and 7% respectively from a year earlier. However, a large proportion of these countries’ shipments to China are so-called intermediate goods, such as electronic components, that are assembled into finished products – often for re-export to developed world demand centres. As such, the underlying cause of weak exports is more likely to be poor demand for consumer goods in the West, especially Europe. **Japan Manufacturing PMI South Korea Manufacturing PMI** 70 70

**Few signs of improvement** Given that consumer demand in Europe and North America is likely to remain subdued over the coming months, there is little reason to expect Asian export shipments to bounce back quickly. Indeed, lead indicators such as the ‘new export orders’ component of the manufacturing PMIs support this view, remaining in contractionary territory in Japan, Korea and Taiwan. This signifies the balance of manufacturers are seeing export orders shrink. As such, we expect industrial growth in developed Asia to remain muted into early 2013.
